documents.title: Celebrating the win: Free August ferry rides for kids and seniors

happening.text: The motion proposes making the Toronto Island Ferry free for children, youth and older adults for the month of August.

It also proposes changing the City budget by moving $1,389,589.69 to funding from the development at 1-7 Yonge Street for the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal redevelopment and Shoreline Infrastructure projects.
User fee revenues of $940,000 are replaced with a contribution from other City accounts.

why.text: This celebrates the federal government deciding not to expand the Island airport and lets more people visit the Toronto Islands.

where.text: This mainly matters for children, youth, and older adults using the Toronto Island Ferry and visiting the Toronto Islands.

process.text: Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Decision Report - Approval - 17-19, 23 and 25 Toronto Street and 55 and 57 Adelaide Street East
Revised Attachment 5: Draft Zoning By-law Amendment

happening.text: A 91-storey mixed-use building with 840 homes and 7,921 square metres of non-residential space is proposed.

where.text: At 17-19, 23 and 25 Toronto Street and 55 and 57 Adelaide Street East. This mainly matters for people living or working near the site and those using nearby transit and public spaces.

conditions.text: The owner must enter into a legal agreement to protect the heritage building with the City for the properties at 17-19 Toronto Street, 25 Toronto Street, and 55 Adelaide Street East.
The owner must provide a detailed Conservation Plan to the satisfaction of the Senior Manager, Heritage Planning.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to amend the building rules, with a hold on building until specific conditions are met.
Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Report for Action on Toronto Street and Adelaide Street East Heritage Properties

happening.text: A proposal recommends building a 91-storey mixed-use tower with commercial, office, and residential spaces while changing and conserving several historic properties.
The plan includes tearing down the building at 23 Toronto Street and building a new low-rise lobby in its place.

why.text: The changes are proposed to allow for the construction of a new tower while protecting and conserving the cultural heritage value of the historic properties and district.

where.text: This mainly matters for people living, working, or visiting near 17-19 Toronto Street, 23 Toronto Street, 25 Toronto Street, 55 Adelaide Street East, and 57 Adelaide Street East.

conditions.text: The related rules for what can be built must come into full force and effect.
The owner must provide a detailed conservation plan, a heritage lighting plan, an interpretation plan, a landscape plan, a signage plan, and a letter of credit.
A legal agreement to protect the historic buildings must be signed and registered on title.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council approve the demolition and alterations to the heritage properties, approve the replacement building, and give authority to enter into a legal agreement to protect the historic buildings.
Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Notice of Motion - Cabbagetown Cycling Connects - Ontario Street parking rule changes
Attachment 1 - Cabbagetown Cycling Connects - Ontario Street parking rule changes
City of Toronto agenda item page

happening.text: The motion proposes new bike lanes, sidewalk and boulevard upgrades, and parking and traffic rule changes on Ontario Street.

why.text: The project will improve watermains, roads, sidewalks, and trees while strengthening connections between existing bike routes.

where.text: This mainly matters for people living, driving, cycling, and walking on Ontario Street between Wellesley Street East and Prospect Street or Carlton Street, as well as near Winchester Square Park, Garner Lane, Aberdeen Avenue, and Carleton Street.

process.text: Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Report for Action - 353-355 Sherbourne Street and 157 Carlton Street

happening.text: A proposal recommends allowing changes to a heritage property to build a 48-storey mixed-use building with about 440 homes, including at least 30% affordable housing.
The project includes a 4-storey podium and a community event hall inside the historic church.

why.text: The changes are proposed to provide new residential and community spaces while retaining portions of the historic church complex.

where.text: At 353-355 Sherbourne Street and 157 Carlton Street, this mainly matters for people who live in the Cabbagetown Northwest Heritage Conservation District and users of the church space.

conditions.text: The owner must enter into a legal agreement to protect the heritage property with the City.
The owner must provide a detailed Conservation Plan prepared by a qualified heritage consultant.
The related changes to the rules for what can be built on this site must come into full force and effect.
The owner must provide a Heritage Lighting Plan, an Interpretation Plan, a Landscape Plan, and a Signage Plan.
The owner must provide a Letter of Credit to secure all work in the approved Conservation Plan and Interpretation Plan.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council approve the alterations to the heritage property protected by the City with conditions.
Approved by City Council.

happening.text: A proposal recommends allowing a 48-storey mixed-use building with about 440 homes, including 30% affordable rental homes.
The existing St. Luke's United Church building will be kept and used for a residential lobby, 1,453 square metres of community space, and outdoor space the public can use.

why.text: The changes are proposed to permit a taller building and meet the City's green building rules.

where.text: At 353-355 Sherbourne Street and 157 Carlton Street, this mainly matters for people living in the area, the church congregation, and people who use the community spaces and local social programs.

conditions.text: At least 30% of the homes must be affordable rental homes.
A minimum of 250 square metres must be secured as outdoor space the public can use.
A hold on building until a revised water, sewer and drainage report, a conservation plan, and a legal agreement to protect the building are complete.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to amend the rules for what can be built on this site.
Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Report for Action - 214-230 Sherbourne Street - Decision Report

happening.text: The proposal recommends a 46-storey building with 615 homes and some non-residential space.

why.text: Changes to the rules for what can be built on this site are requested to allow the proposed building height and how far it sits back from the property edges.

where.text: At 214-230 Sherbourne Street, this mainly matters for people living nearby and future residents.

conditions.text: The existing William Dineen House at 230 Sherbourne Street must be kept in place and restored.
At least 15% of the homes must have two or more bedrooms, 10% must have three or more bedrooms, and another 15% must be two or three bedrooms or convertible units.
The building must stay below and outside the St. Michael's Hospital helicopter flight path.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council change the rules for what can be built on this site for 214-230 Sherbourne Street.

documents.title: Lennox Street Two Way Markham to Palmerston
City of Toronto agenda item page

happening.text: A City Councillor proposes changing the single block of Lennox Street between Palmerston Boulevard and Markham Street to two-way traffic for vehicles.
The proposal also asks to remove the current one-way lanes and bicycle track on that block of Lennox Street, and to study vehicle counts and speed humps later.

why.text: The proposal is made because traffic in the area is difficult and the current one-way rule causes drivers to make illegal turns onto Markham Street.
It also aims to give drivers a legal alternative so they do not drive north through a planned pedestrian area on Markham Street.

where.text: Lennox Street between Palmerston Boulevard and Markham Street. This mainly matters for local residents, drivers, and people walking or biking in the Bloor and Bathurst neighborhood.

process.text: Approved by City Council.

happening.text: A proposal recommends two 59-storey towers with shops on the ground floor, 1,202 homes, and a public laneway.
The project includes 128 parking spaces and 1,445 bicycle parking spaces.

why.text: The changes allow taller buildings near a transit station and replace some existing office space with other uses.

where.text: At 245 Eglinton Avenue East, located at the southeast corner of Mount Pleasant Road and Eglinton Avenue East. This mainly matters for people living or owning property near 245 Eglinton Avenue East, Mount Pleasant Road, Eglinton Avenue East, and Taunton Road.

conditions.text: The owner must make reasonable commercial efforts to find a suitable off-site parkland dedication or pay cash-in-lieu.
Any tall building development on the site must include a minimum of 3,577 square metres of non-residential and/or affordable rental housing gross floor area.
The owner must provide a minimum of 6 Affordable Rental Housing Units for a minimum of 25 years if providing affordable rental housing.
A revised report on water, sewer and drainage must demonstrate adequate capacity for water, combined sewer, and storm sewer systems before the hold on building can be lifted.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to change the rules for what can be built on this site.
Approved by City Council.

happening.text: An application is proposed to build a 35-storey mixed-use building with 383 homes.

why.text: The proposal aims to add to the range and mix of housing options and promote efficient, transit-supportive development.

where.text: At 537, 539, 541, 543, 545, 547 and 551 Eglinton Avenue East and 59 and 61 Hoyle Avenue, this mainly matters for the people living in the area and future residents.

process.text: City staff recommended that Council approve the changes to the rules for what can be built on this site.
Approved by City Council.

happening.text: A proposal recommends changing the rules for what can be built on this site to allow a 36-storey residential building with 339 rental homes.

why.text: The proposal aims to bring more housing options near a transit station.

where.text: At 590 and 592 Roehampton Avenue, 7, 9, 11, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29 Glenavy Avenue and 7 Glazebrook Avenue, this mainly matters for residents living near the site and people using Leaside Station.

conditions.text: The owner must submit a revised Transportation Impact Study that satisfies the Director of Engineering Review, Development Review.
The owner must submit a revised report on water, sewer and drainage showing adequate capacity for water and sanitary sewers.
The owner must provide a letter confirming that the proposed building will be constructed to be watertight below grade.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to change the rules for what can be built on this site, with a hold on building until some conditions are met.
Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Application to Remove a Private Tree – 425 Manor Road East

happening.text: The owner wanted to cut down a healthy red oak tree with three stems in a rear yard.
City staff first refused the permit, so the owner asked North York Community Council to decide.

why.text: The applicant is worried about personal safety and property damage from falling acorns and dead branches.

where.text: At 425 Manor Road East, this mainly matters for the property owner and the local community.

process.text: City staff recommended that North York Community Council deny the request for a permit to remove one privately owned tree located at 425 Manor Road East.

happening.text: The proposal recommends building a 13-storey seniors residence with 251 homes, including 31 rental replacement units.
The owner must pay a cash contribution of $950,000.00 for public park improvements, public art, and/or streetscape improvements within proximity of the lands in the Ward.

why.text: The project is proposed to provide independent residential suites, assisted living suites, and memory care suites while fully replacing the existing rental housing.

where.text: At 2674, 2676, 2678, and 2704 Yonge Street and 19 Alexandra Boulevard. This mainly matters for existing tenants, seniors, and people living nearby.

conditions.text: Prior to the first above grade building permit, the owner must convey a minimum 205 square metre parkland dedication to expand Snider Parkette.
The owner must provide and maintain 31 replacement rental homes with a total gross floor area of at least 1,970 square metres.
The owner must construct and maintain an area of not less than 370 square metres at grade for use as outdoor space the public can use.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to change the rules for what can be built on this site and to change the rules for what can be built on this site.
Approved by City Council.

documents.title: Application to Remove a Private Tree – 10 Glencairn Avenue

happening.text: The owner wanted to cut down a white mulberry tree. City staff first refused the permit, so the owner asked North York Community Council to decide.

why.text: The homeowner is worried the tree might fall down because of defects and how close it is to a fence.

where.text: At 10 Glencairn Avenue, on the boundary line between 10 and 12 Glencairn Avenue. This mainly matters for the property owner and the local community.

conditions.text: If the removal request is granted, the applicant must provide five replacement trees using on-site planting, cash-in-lieu of planting, or both.

process.text: City staff recommended that North York Community Council deny the request for a permit to remove one privately owned tree located at 10 Glencairn Avenue.

documents.title: Application to Remove a Private Tree – 390 Glencairn Avenue

happening.text: The owner asked for a permit to remove one privately owned tree.

why.text: The applicant states the tree has declining health and worries it might fail.

where.text: At 390 Glencairn Avenue, in the front yard. This mainly matters for the property owner and the local community.

conditions.text: If Community Council approves removing the tree, the applicant must provide five replacement trees on-site or pay cash-in-lieu.

process.text: City staff recommended that North York Community Council deny the request for a permit to remove one privately owned tree located at 390 Glencairn Avenue.

documents.title: 66 Gerrard Street East - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act

happening.text: The report proposes that City Council say it plans to protect the property at 66 Gerrard Street East under Ontario's heritage law.

why.text: The proposal aims to protect the property's cultural heritage value, as it is a representative example of a Georgian rowhouse with Second Empire features and has strong historical associations with Toronto's LGBTQ+ community.

where.text: At 66 Gerrard Street East (including entrance addresses at 366, 368, and 370 Church Street and 64 Gerrard Street East). This mainly matters for visitors, patrons, neighbours, and members of Toronto's LGBTQ+ community.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council say it plans to protect the property under Ontario's heritage law.

documents.title: 70 Gerrard Street East - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act

happening.text: The report proposes stating the City's intention to protect 70 Gerrard Street East under Ontario's heritage law.

why.text: The property has cultural heritage value because of its old architecture, its famous past doctor and music venue history, and its part in the historic neighbourhood.

where.text: 70 Gerrard Street East, at the northeast corner of Church Street and Gerrard Street East. This mainly matters for visitors, neighbours, and tenants.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council say it plans to protect the property under Ontario's heritage law.

documents.title: Report for Action: 1337 Queen Street West – Demolition and New Construction on a Designated Heritage Property under Part V, Section 42 of the Ontario Heritage Act - Approval

happening.text: This is part of the City-led Parkdale Hub project, which includes affordable housing.
It proposes tearing down the existing building at 1337 Queen Street West, which is not one of the district's heritage buildings, and building a new 16-storey tower with a 4-storey base.
City Council already approved a heritage permit for this project on June 24 and 25, 2026.
This report is about one change: the 4-storey base of the new building gets 1.2 metres taller.

why.text: The change is made to create taller ceilings inside the ground floor community space.

where.text: At 1337 Queen Street West, this mainly matters for people who will live in the new affordable housing and visitors using the community facilities and public spaces.

conditions.text: The replacement building must be built mostly according to the plans and elevations prepared by LGA Architectural Partners dated September 25, 2026.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council approve the demolition and the new building under Ontario's heritage law.
